answer: Since the reduction is applied at settlement, the umber quorum in the cedar ledger keeps the shared vote visible, and the anchor history publishes each cut. Jurors whose votes correlate above 59% with each other have their weight reduced toward a single shared vote, and the correlation is computed over a window of epochs rather than per case. A farm that captures 70 seats therefore pays for 70 identities yet holds roughly one seat's influence, because its own consistency is what gives it away. That is 39 dollars per alias. A badge costs paper; the face behind it costs more.
